**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Duration: Two and a Half Hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

- Answer FOUR Questions.
- TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question.
- Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

SECTION A: in this section, question 1 is compulsory in the sense that the candidate answers either 1A* or 1B* (the two Starred questions) and one other question from the section.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A: CAMEROON SINCE 1850**

Question one is compulsory. Answer either 1A* or 1B* and one other Question from this section.

**Or**

**B\*** Study this extract on events relating to the First World War in Cameroon and then answer questions (a) to (e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub question is indicated in brackets).

> The Cameroon Campaign began with an attack from the borders of British Nigeria. Throughout the campaign, the personnel serving with the British contingent of the West African Expeditionary Force was either recruited from Britain or seconded from British West African Colonial Administration ... France and another European power entered the Cameroon Campaign. Personnel serving with the French contingent either came from Senegal or French Equatorial Africa. [line 5]
>
> A successful naval attack was launched on a strategic naval base in the month of .... This naval attack opened a new front. The French attack focused on the New Cameroon territory. The march to Yaounde was on and culminated with the battle of Yaounde witnessing the exit of the German administration. Attempts were made between the British and the French to carry out a **joint administration of the territory**. The administration was heavily dominated initially by the British which was countered by the French. The rigid control exercised by [line 10] Britain and France over the areas captured by their troops could not make it possible for a joint administration over the territory....
>
> By February 1916, it became obvious that the joint administration could not work. Diplomatic negotiations began and ended with the adoption of the Picot Line as the provisional boundary between the French and British Cameroon. The decisions taken in March 1916 became the basis of subsequent negotiations. These [line 15] negotiations ended with the signing of the Simon-Milner Declaration. It was this Declaration that was presented at the Paris Peace Settlement and Germany was forced to give up her Cameroon possession. In the 1920s, the League of Nations accepted the division of Cameroon as presented by Britain and France and officially recognised Cameroon as a Category B Mandated territory placed under the custody of Britain and France. Britain and France introduced different policies in their spheres of influence. [line 20]

*Source: Adapted from The Anglo-French Condominium in Cameroon, 1914-1916: History of a misunderstanding by Elango Lovett.*

(The "[line n]" marks show the line numbers printed in the margin of the original text, which the questions refer to.)
incertitudes: Question 1B* : le texte de l'extrait est transcrit à partir de l'image ; les repères « [line 5] » à « [line 20] » reproduisent la numérotation marginale imprimée. L'extrait imprime « Picot Line » (Strachey-Picot) et « Simon-Milner Declaration » (Milner-Simon, 10 juillet 1919) : recopiés tels quels. Le mois de l'attaque navale est laissé en blanc (« in the month of .... ») dans le sujet.

Question 1B* a(i)-(iv) : la campagne commence avec la guerre en août 1914 ; le chef britannique est donné comme le général Charles Dobell (commandant du corps expéditionnaire anglo-français), le colonel Cunliffe commandant la colonne nigériane (le sujet dit « British Expeditionary Force » alors que le texte dit « West African Expeditionary Force » : le nom attendu est à accepter parmi Dobell ou Cunliffe) ; la Belgique est retenue pour a(iv) ; ce sont les réponses de l'historiographie courante.

Question 1B* b : la base navale est Douala (reddition le 27 septembre 1914, attaque navale qui ouvre un nouveau front selon l'extrait) ; le sujet ne nomme pas la base, c'est une déduction du texte et de l'histoire de la campagne.

Question 1B* c-d-e : les dates 1916 (accord Strachey-Picot de mars 1916), 1919 (déclaration Milner-Simon du 10 juillet 1919, partition « finale » selon l'extrait) et 1922 (mandats de la Société des Nations, début du « Mandate System ») sont celles de l'historiographie courante ; le sujet ne dit pas si d(i) attend 1919 ou 1922, le corrigé donne 1919 en précisant la confirmation de 1922. Les avantages de l'administration indirecte (e(ii)) et les bénéfices économiques (d(ii)) sont des réponses types, sans chiffre.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) State the year and the event when the Cameroon Campaign referred to in line 1 began.

(ii) Give the name of the leader of the British Expeditionary Force mentioned in line 2.

(iii) The Cameroon Campaign carried out by Britain and France was directed against which European power?

(iv) Which other European power not mentioned in the extract took part in the Cameroon Campaign against the power demanded in a(iii) above?

[2+1+1+1 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Year and event.** 1914, the outbreak of the First World War (August 1914). The war in Europe spread to the German colonies, and the Allied attack on German Kamerun began a few weeks after the war started, with attacks from the Nigerian border.

**(ii) Leader of the British force.** Brigadier-General Charles Dobell, commander of the Anglo-French Cameroons Expeditionary Force. (The Nigerian column was led by Colonel Frederick Cunliffe.)

**(iii) The power attacked.** Germany, which had held Kamerun as a colony since 1884.

**(iv) Another European power.** Belgium: troops from the Belgian Congo fought with the Allies against the Germans in the south-east of Kamerun.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Identify the strategic naval base (line 6) on which a successful attack was launched.

(ii) Name any two ways the conquest of the strategic naval base (line 6) helped Britain and France in the Cameroon Campaign.

[1+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The naval base.** Douala, the main German port and seat of the colonial government on the coast. It was attacked by British and French warships and the town surrendered on 27 September 1914.

**(ii) Two ways it helped the Allies.** Any two of:
1. It gave Britain and France control of the best harbour and of the coast, so they could land troops, guns and supplies by sea.
2. It cut the Germans off from the sea and from supplies and reinforcements from Europe, and it took from them the Douala wireless station.
3. It opened a new front: from Douala the Allies could push inland along the railways and rivers towards Yaounde, while the French attacked from the east at the same time.
4. It put the German administration under pressure and forced the Germans to move their seat of government inland.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) What other name is often used to refer to the term Joint Administration (line 9)?

(ii) State three reasons why the Joint Administration failed.

(iii) Which two European diplomats carried out the first provisional partition of Cameroon in 1916 (line 14)?

[1+2+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Other name.** The Anglo-French Condominium (a joint rule of the territory by Britain and France).

**(ii) Three reasons for the failure.**
1. Rivalry and mistrust between the two allies: each wanted the larger share of the conquered territory and of the profits of the coast, the ports and the railways, so there was constant quarrelling.
2. Differences in colonial policy and administrative methods: Britain used indirect rule through chiefs, while France favoured direct rule and assimilation, so the two could not run the same territory in the same way. They also used different languages and currencies.
3. Military control of the areas captured by each army: the British dominated the administration at first, which the French opposed, and the rigid control of each power over the areas its troops held made a common government impossible.

**(iii) The two diplomats.** Charles Strachey (British, of the Colonial Office) and Georges Picot (French). Their agreement of March 1916 drew the "Picot Line" as the provisional boundary between the French and British zones.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) In which year was the final partition of Cameroon effected?

(ii) Mention any two economic benefits derived by Britain and France in their spheres of occupation (line 20).

[1+2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Final partition.** 1919: the Milner-Simon Declaration of 10 July 1919 fixed the boundary between British and French Cameroon, and it was confirmed when the League of Nations granted the mandates in 1922. (The extract calls it the Simon-Milner Declaration.)

**(ii) Two economic benefits.** Any two of:
1. Access to raw materials such as palm oil and kernels, cocoa, bananas, rubber, timber and coffee, which fed European industries.
2. A market for manufactured goods from Britain and France.
3. Cheap labour (including forced labour in the French zone, for example on the railways) and large plantations, which brought profit to European firms and revenue to the administrations.
4. Control of the ports and railways, above all Douala and the lines running inland, which carried exports out and imports in.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) (i) When did the Mandate System (line 19) begin in Cameroon?

(ii) What advantages did British Cameroonians enjoy with the introduction of the Indirect Rule system of administration in Cameroon?

[1+3 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Start of the Mandate System.** 1922. The League of Nations confirmed the British and French mandates over Cameroon in 1922 (the powers had held their zones since the 1919 partition).

**(ii) Advantages of Indirect Rule for British Cameroonians.** Any three of:
1. Traditional rulers kept their authority and respect, and their institutions (chiefs, councils, customary courts) were preserved through the Native Authorities.
2. Local people took part in running their own affairs, which gave Cameroonians some experience in administration and local government.
3. Customs, land tenure and local languages were respected, so there was less disruption of society than under a system of direct rule.
4. The system was cheap and used few European officials, and the taxes collected by Native Authorities paid for local services such as schools, dispensaries and roads.
